entry.title: Working CV Is About Consistency
entry.content:
Intro

Looking for a job can be so challenging that it takes a mental toll on us, and we tend to avoid this irritating task of reviewing and editing the CV one more time. Even when we read the CV, it can be overwhelming to stick to the goals. And the CV has only one goal – to get you in the door, or, in other words, to get you to the first interview round, which is usually with HR. HR people don't know anything about your job, especially if you are well qualified in your field – so well that it's hard for anyone outside your field to understand what you are actually doing. So HR people tend to concentrate on the 10% of the CV they can understand and whether the overall picture is taking shape:

  1. What was your career path?
  2. What did you achieve and what were you actually paid for?
  3. What do you do well and want to do in your next job?

These are tough questions, as your career path can be non-linear, with movements back and forth, career breaks for many different reasons, and jobs you did well but are no longer willing to do. Well, I don't have the statistics on hand, but I think this is a common case, so the task here is to make it look linear, even if it isn't. Why linear? Well, human beings follow linear stories best, and your CV is your story. Your next job should look like a logical next chapter of this story. And storytelling is hard, make no mistake about that. Stories that only scratch the surface don't touch anyone, so this should be a story about how you found your passion and followed it despite all the obstacles. Mistakes along the way are actually advantages because they mean you risked something, gained experience, and are persistent enough to follow your path further. I would hire a person like that. Let's start from the inside.

Finding your passion

First, there are a lot of great books on the topic, and if the tip below doesn't do you any good, just go out there and find some information. The only thing I'm sure about is that you shouldn't approach work without passion, because passion indicates that you have high expectations and are ready to invest your time and energy to get what you expect – so you're just waiting for the tasks. And my tip would probably work best for people with some work experience. For students and schoolkids, I'd definitely recommend getting some experience; the best time is probably a year after finishing school. But let's get back on track.

So, here's the story. It was an interview at a mining company with an almost nonexistent project culture (in terms of business transformation) and some red flags regarding the internal atmosphere. But it was a functioning business anyway, and they somehow managed to get some stuff done on a large scale. And the manager asked me this question: Who are you? I was surprised by this direct question, and it made me reply without questioning myself: I'm a consultant. I had worked as a consultant before and felt emotionally and professionally in the right place in that role. The point was that they didn't have consultants; they had managers who took full responsibility, so I obviously didn't fit. If your answer is "I don't know", that's fine, as long as you're passionately looking for your place in life, the place where you bring value to society and are happy about it. In a case I saw recently, three different roles were mixed in one CV, and obviously, only one of them reflected that person's passion. Just ask yourself.

Cutting the excess

I assume that a CV is a 100% functional document: it should get you in the door; that's its only function. It works or it's worthless, and people tend to forget about that. It's not a monument to your life, it's not about describing all the experiences you've had, and it's not about showing the world what a multifaceted person you are. It doesn't need to look nice or smart, so if you're hesitating over whether it makes sense to edit your latest "holy" version, which you like so much, just ask yourself: Did it get you interviews? If it didn't, edit it now.

Obviously, you need to match your skill set and experience with the positions on the market, and I know exactly two approaches that work here. The first is resource-consuming, and you need some skills to do market research. So you analyze the open positions, probably the economic situation as well, to calculate your chances. Then you tailor your CV to target a particular segment and go for it. At this stage, you probably know the words used in job titles and descriptions, and that's a serious advantage. The second approach is hypothesis testing: you say, "This job probably exists, and I could do it." It seems that the chances of guessing correctly are low, but I prefer this method because I get feedback quickly and collect valuable information. You probably won't succeed in the first iteration, but the information you get will allow you to tailor your CV faster.

And tailoring is the key word here. It means cutting everything that distracts attention from your target role. I compressed the first five years of my career, during which I worked at different companies and completed very challenging projects, into one sentence because otherwise I got only roles as a Microsoft Dynamics consultant, and I had decided to go into management consulting. It's hard to overcome the emotional attachment to those years of my career, but in that case, it was worth it, and I got what I wanted. Bonus tip: it allowed me to cut my CV to one page, and I got more interviews because HR people were kind of intrigued by this short version.

Making it consistent

A very special HR tip is that HR people are just normal people reading your CV, so they can't understand your highly specialized professional stuff, but they can understand inconsistencies that any human being can spot:

  • Jumping between manager, sales, and specialist roles
  • Mixing what you delivered (the business results) with the process that led to it
  • Having more than three bullet points for each role

You see, I could write about many more inconsistencies, but I chose the three most important ones because there's a magic trick behind the way people process information in series of three. An inconsistency can also reveal itself in how you write about different positions: if some of them are described in more detail, you're probably hiding something about the others. And if the style is different (the language, the rhythm, even the grammar), you simply haven't done your homework and haven't read the CV yourself to make it consistent. It's just about respecting the other party, the reader: they shouldn't have any difficulties reading your CV from beginning to end. Nothing should stick out or catch their attention if it shouldn't. Just pretend for a moment that you're the reader and read it one more time. Mark all the inconsistencies ruthlessly, then take one more iteration to correct them. For some psychological reason, a printed CV works better for this exercise because you don't switch to "editing" mode immediately.

Making it work

That wasn't easy, but that's not all there is to it. The hardest part is this: if it were your job to hire this person, would you do it? If the answer is no, you probably need some more iterations. But if you just send your CV "as is", you close the doors (the opportunities) yourself, because you can send your CV only once. There is some reasoning behind people just spamming others with their CV: it's better than doing nothing, I'll be noticed at least – and so on. But "at least" is not enough. You either get the attention you need to be invited to an interview, or you don't. Many things can go wrong, starting with the CV format, the words you use, or the job market, but, all other things being equal, I'd hire a person who acts reasonably in a stressful situation over a person who goes into full panic mode. I'd actually prefer a reasonable person with a huge handicap in skills and experience. There was a reason to put "Don't Panic" on the cover of The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, you know.

Conclusions

If I were to write a history of the present time, I'd describe it as a time of transition, and it's the hardest time to live in (probably not that hard compared to times without the Internet and toilet paper). We are stressed because we know something has changed, but we don't know how to adapt, or adapting is too painful: it seems that you need some black magic to satisfy LinkedIn algorithms and AI, which won't let your CV reach a human. And I just don't buy it: if a company can't choose a functioning AI, I don't want to work for that company, because they have probably made some other bad management decisions. The same goes for using strange LinkedIn features or hiring unprofessional HR people. How do I deal with this craziness? I deal only with reasonable people. My motto is: if the world goes crazy, it doesn't mean I have to. But communicating your strengths to sentient people is important and worth investing some effort in, from my perspective. I also assume that the percentage of craziness is constant; it's just more visible now.

entry.title: What Intranet Is Actually For
entry.content:
Intro

I remember the early 2000s (yes, I'm that old), which I would call a romantic time, when the Internet was full of intellectuals, companies invested a lot in Intranet, and you could have everything you wanted there: buy and sell stuff, discuss your superiors, and the like. I'd call the time we live in cynical, with a COVID pandemic behind us, when we lost that "just for fun" © nerdy feeling of doing cool stuff just because we can. I see that management refuses to invest a little time in building the Intranet, even when it costs them literally nothing in terms of IT resources. And I try to comprehend the reasoning behind that: COVID reminded us that business is about making money, which people are free to spend on whatever makes them happy. And yet I see particular reasons to have an Intranet, on the one hand, and the reasoning of companies trying to make products in this area completely missing the point, on the other. Let's look at Open Intranet, for example. The features are compactly listed on their GitHub. Everything is very down-to-earth and even technical, but I see some very different reasons to have an Intranet.

Why, finally

The right question is missing here in the first place, from my point of view, and that is: what are you not able to have without an Intranet? And the follow-up: what could you significantly improve with an Intranet? Let's get into my arguments:

  • A company is a group of people spending a lot of time together (even remotely), and just acknowledging this fact is valuable. Like, who we are, what's going on, I mean events, birthdays, news, and photos from events as well. Just don't let HR and PR get into this; write it yourself.
  • We tend to use more web apps nowadays, and just having a single page with a collection of links and short descriptions can make a difference.
  • I don't hate email anymore, but I don't accept it as a primary communication channel. You can put anything you want in emails, but if people need to use it further, please be so kind as to post it on some website in an accessible way.
  • Onboarding is a process worth revisiting, and whatever you write, whether a PDF, a PowerPoint presentation, or a simple webpage (way better), please keep it updated and accessible for newcomers, because the first few weeks can be hard.
  • I'll skip the document library, but I'm personally interested in some space for the project team to post documents and updates on what's going on (or at least to show that we're still alive as a project). It makes a difference, especially for long-term projects, and it's even covered in project management books (if communication management rings a bell).

I'm not selling anything, so I'll not waste your time (or the precious bytes of my blog) convincing you that the reasons above are important. I'm personally convinced that every bullet point deserves an article, as each brings value (again, it depends on how you cook it), and they are not corporate BS. It's low-hanging fruit to make life a little bit easier for people at work, because it serves a greater purpose: how we, human beings, exchange information with each other and how we treat each other. Why is it low-hanging fruit? Well...

The tools

Most companies already have SharePoint, as it's included even in the cheapest Microsoft 365 cloud subscription, and I think it's a great place to start. It's bad; I curse Microsoft every time I use it. The last time I specifically remember, I had to reload the page every time I saved because it went blank. But hear me out: SharePoint has three massive advantages:

  • You most likely already have it, as I've mentioned before, and that's still important.
  • It is integrated into group and policy management, so it's easy to have a closed, protected Intranet and manage access rights – and that can be less straightforward with other systems. Plus, you get Windows authentication out of the box, and users will thank you.
  • It is integrated with Teams and OneDrive, so you can put a link to a file and edit it in one place.

SharePoint also gets the job done in terms of, well, creating webpages, and it's kind of OK at that. Blogging is easy (and underappreciated for corporate communications, as I see it). You can also integrate forms, and they'll save info to an Excel table, just exactly how you'd expect it. And I've solved a lot of real-world tasks with just three tools, but you can find more if you dig deeper. Some are trash by default, including Loop, by the way. Just stick to the basics, and you'll be fine.

But SharePoint would be my second choice, even after default Drupal. Drupal is beautiful, safe, scalable, fast, and automates the publishing process the right way. Again, start by automating the publishing process itself and have some fun along the way. Open Intranet (see the links above) adds everything you dreamed of, so it's definitely worth visiting. Regarding extensions, I would start with the most boring, hated, and overlooked stuff – notably, authentication. That's because nowadays you still have to authenticate everywhere, although this problem has already been solved. It's about respecting your users, sorry, employees. Wiki and document management seem promising; I'm just too spoiled by specialized solutions. Maybe it'll do; I don't know. Must-read posts and GDPR definitely arouse the interest of a compliance department, if your company is big enough to have one. So, yes, you could meet a lot of requirements with one product.

Conclusion

Finding the right balance is hard, especially with communication. Take informal chats, for example: the best examples I've seen were selected chats where people could go nuts with the jokes – if you don't appreciate it, just quit the chat. But it should also fit in with the corporate culture, and these two words could go wrong in so many ways. And an Intranet is just a tool for transmitting this corporate culture, and that could go wrong in too many ways as well. So I see the point of not taking the risks, especially if your company is in survival mode. But I've convinced myself that having fun while working positively influences the atmosphere and everything else I do, so I don't struggle with this choice anymore – I'd definitely go for it.

entry.title: A Capable Road Bike
entry.content:
Intro

I was (not very happily) riding my MTB, and I realized that I wanted to ride further, as the MTB started to feel slow and uncomfortable after 20 km. Choosing a road bike turned out to be a rabbit hole: a used bike would normally be my go-to option, but some weird stuff happened recently that made this option less attractive. First, technology has really advanced, and I see no point in buying a €300 bike with outdated 28mm tires (pretty uncomfortable; I've used them), ball bearings (I've used them as well, and they sucked), and a frame that didn't allow me to solve the tire problem. On the other hand, the COVID bike boom led to overproduction, so €1200 – the price of a decent new bike – is now the starting price for a used bike. The technical details and options started to feel overwhelming, so I had to stop and figure out my requirements.

Requirements

I definitely wanted to get modern tech if it was beneficial for me, and I didn't want to pay for stuff I wasn't going to use. The idea is to ride the bike on paved roads occasionally for recreation (for now, 40 km rides at a speed of about 25 km/h), and I'm also thinking about going on longer rides with some luggage while on vacation. So I'm definitely not buying:

  • Carbon frames: they're almost a scam in terms of durability, and there's no way to fit a standard bike rack on them.
  • Gravel bikes: on paved roads, they just mean extra weight.
  • Bikepacking gear: all of it seems questionable to me when I can just use standard panniers.

What I actually want is a road bike with drop handlebars to be able to change my riding position, along with the following features:

  • Sealed bearings
  • Thru-axles, because they're just better
  • Aluminum frame with mounting points for a standard bike rack
  • Disc brakes, as they provide tire clearance and are easy to set up
  • 32 mm tires by default
  • Internal cable routing, as it looks a lot nicer
  • Carbon fork, as it's lightweight and absorbs vibrations

If you dig deeper into pricing, you'll find out that the price of a bike is largely determined by the frame and the groupset, and most brands use only Shimano or SRAM. Their prices are rather high, so some companies have started using Microshift. It turned out that at least the Microshift Sword is a decent groupset and better than Shimano Claris, an entry-level groupset from Shimano. I've used it for four months, and all I can say is that it shifts well, although I haven't tested other groupsets. Since it's relatively new, you won't be able to find used bikes equipped with it. So I ended up buying a new Van Rysel Endurance Rennrad EDR AF Microshift Sword 2x10 for well below the aforementioned €1200.

Pros and cons

Let's get to the pros and cons first, and after that, let's talk about how you can push your costs down even further. So, the pros:

  • Satisfies all my requirements
  • It's obviously very cheap
  • Surprisingly good assembly quality
  • Rides well; I actually feel like riding it more
  • I didn't need to replace any components other than the saddle

The cons do exist, though:

  • The included lights and standard tools suck
  • The bike doesn't make me coffee :)

Since we're talking about a road bike, it makes sense to get clipless pedals, so I didn't think twice about choosing Shimano SPD. You quickly find out that shoes for these pedals cost a lot, but Decathlon has a Van Rysel option that is cheap and does the job. They also have SPD-compatible pedals, but I didn't think it was worth cutting corners there.

Bike racks can also vary a lot in price, anywhere from €30 to €150. Decathlon saves the day again here by offering reliable, low-cost options. After buying all the gear, I was even able to order good lights using just my bonus points. It doesn't end there: you'll probably need a frame bag for tools, glasses, and clothing (I wear a helmet, by the way), plus a bike lock. When you sum everything up, you can save a fortune with Decathlon – and I'm not even affiliated with them.

That's not all, because Decathlon also offers a variety of payment options that you don't get when buying a used bike from someone. By the way, Decathlon has a section for used bikes, but I couldn't find any attractive offers there.

Conclusion

I won't lie, though – there are some caveats with modern tech:

  • Internal cable routing requires more work when replacing cables
  • Thru-axles are worse if you intend to use a bike trailer
  • Front derailleurs are generally not recommended by some people because they tend not to work well

Well, I'm quite happy and not thinking about upgrades for now. That's the whole point – to ride rather than look for new stuff to buy. If I had a bigger budget, I would go for an aluminum bike from Rose. Alternatively, Canyon offers a surprisingly affordable carbon bike, but I'd need to spend at least €80 on an Orbea bike rack. Those are good options, though, and I'm sure a lot of people are happy with them. The point is that all the tech is essentially the same; geometry and components do make a difference, but not for my use case. The frame fits well, by the way, which is really important, although the riding position feels more relaxed and neutral than aggressive. It's a road bike, at the end of the day, not a race bike.

entry.title: Solving It On the Front-end
entry.content:
Requirements

As an input we have a website with some PDFs (documentation) for various modules and versions of some software in German and in English. We actually don't know:

  • If all the docs exist for the latest version
  • If the docs are duplicated in the different folders using different filenames
  • If the docs are available only in one language or in both

As I'll be the one using these docs, I thought of an HTML page with an integrated search where there's a table with the following fields:

  • Doc type
  • Doc name (the actual title, not the filename)
  • Link to the English version
  • Link to the German version

That sounds reasonable, right? Let's get into it then.

The tools

The idea is to export all the information into Excel and do some matching there, then identify the duplicates, delete them, and finally create the resulting page.

The actual process involved choosing the tools along the way, but at the end I've got this:

  • Chrome extension to scan the page and download all PDFs
  • Grid.js for the search
  • Pico CSS, because I like the nice and accessible look (it's used on this website as well)
  • Some custom JavaScript to make Pico CSS styles work for Grid.js
  • Some custom JavaScript to output the link to the file in the EN and DE columns
  • Some CLI commands like ls and find to create the list of the files
  • pdfinfo to extract the "Title" metadata from PDFs, if available (combined with some bash scripting)
  • xargs with rm to remove the files from the list
  • A few sed commands to clean the CSV file saved in Excel from some Windows-specific symbols
  • csv2list, a custom Python script to convert the result in Excel into the "list of lists" format required by Grid.js
  • list2csv, a custom Python script for conversion backwards
  • Excel for basic VLOOKUP operations and manual fixes

The sequence

I had to do some back-and-forth movements, so it took me about a day to make 300 lines from 600 files, but for the future I would do something like this:

  1. Download all the files
  2. Create a CSV with filename + folder and name (title) columns
  3. Match the files (duplicates, newer version, EN-DE) in Excel
  4. Create in Excel the list of files to remove and save to txt
  5. Remove the files with xargs + txt
  6. Save the table from Excel to CSV
  7. Convert CSV to list of lists

It works quite well, and combined with fast Chrome rendering and an ability to open PDFs directly in the browser, it looks like a solid solution.

Conclusions

I'm not a programmer, so I asked an AI chatbot to do the heavy lifting with the programming. You still need to understand the Python or JS code it produces, and bash scripts are particularly dangerous. Looking back, I'd just move slower and more systematically to eliminate manual work and associated mistakes as much as possible. Well, you can't know everything in advance. I thought it was a 2-hour task, but I'm still happy with the result every time I use it.

The issue with the static HTML page is that it can work well only in a few cases:

  • From a network folder, accessible to everyone, and when people are disciplined enough to open index.html
  • When an HTTP server delivers it, which requires some setup

For example, to integrate it into SharePoint you would need to create a component and install this component. Which is kind of sad, because I can't see how a static page with some JS can be dangerous.

entry.title: .net 10 Could Hit the Sweet Spot
entry.content:
Intro

A quick recap of previous episodes:

  1. I tried to reflect on programming language development history and the reasoning behind it.
  2. I tried to write some real-world apps using JavaScript and Go.
  3. I still didn't find the unicorn and felt bad about wanting to write more server-side JavaScript.

What fit me well and allowed me to write the most logic per hour was actually Django, because of some embedded stuff like roles, an ORM, security features, user management, and not overloading me with technical stuff. But my requirements emerged, and now I want the following as well:

  • Components on the server-side like JSX
  • CLI tools for standard development tasks
  • Cross-platform with desktop and mobile
  • Consistent language syntax (not like "===" in JS)
  • Probably still object-oriented and compiled

Of course, it should be open-source and permissive to write any apps I want – that's just non-negotiable, but something worth checking when you are dealing with Microsoft.

Go is great – it really pushed me in terms of thinking, but if you take a "machine-human" scale, it's somewhere on the machine part. These are not roadblocks, it just made me realize one more time what I'm capable of:

  • Expressing human logic with Go concepts can be hard, and it's more on the low-level and do-it-yourself end for technical stuff.
  • Go pushes towards a SQL-first approach and away from ORMs, although real-life apps like Gitea do use ORMs to be able to support different DBMSs.

And with all that said, I'm going to try another ecosystem that introduced a few exciting changes recently: .net 10.

.net 10 perks

Actually, .net 10 has got everything from the above, specifically:

  • Components with Razor pages
  • An ORM, Entity Framework Core, supporting a really wide range of DBMSs
  • An open-source web server is there as well
  • C# fits all the requirements for a server-side compiled language with garbage collection, AOT, and co.
  • All the aforementioned "batteries-included" features like role management
  • The courses and documentation are all there

And there's Avalonia for a unified, modern UI across Linux, Windows, and macOS desktop as well as mobile (iOS and Android).

At the moment, I tried to cross-compile a simple desktop app from WSL to Windows, and it worked. I compiled one for Linux, and it worked as well. The drawbacks? Sure:

  • A minimal desktop app was about 200 MB, because .net 10 was included and it's naive to expect that it should be pre-installed; it's the opposite of Go's approach, thus requiring packaging for installation and dependency management, which is different on every platform and Linux distribution. 120 MB without .net, by the way, and I could probably trim that.
  • The language is huge; it would probably take a lot of time to comprehend all of its features and be able to use them.
  • The legacy of being tied to the Microsoft ecosystem, which can still be true for some add-ons; and... Microsoft behaving inconsistently.

Conclusions

I always looked at C# as Java for Microsoft fanboys, but technically it was an effort to make Java normal. The surprise for me is that in .net 10, all the critical components are open-source and cross-platform. Even Microsoft itself hasn't produced apps leveraging all the features of .net 10. Teams could do that, but it has a legacy codebase and is a web-first app, so it makes sense for them to continue struggling with React. Let's review one reason pro and one reason contra.

The reason contra is that I've heard a lot of stories of rewriting Java apps in Go, but I don't know any examples of rewriting a Java app in C# and .net. It's especially strange because C# is similar to Java, while Go is not. What I think is that .net got this critical package of features in .net 10 quite recently, while Google and Go have been consistent for more than 10 years. It's about trust, which is a weak side of Microsoft. Again, what forced Microsoft to make the right choices finally? Maybe they feel they are losing ground, and locking users into their ecosystem is not enough anymore. It's like companies making their tech stack open-source before filing for bankruptcy. And the next question is: will Microsoft remain consistent with open-source components if .net gains traction? With the reputation Microsoft built (or destroyed) over the years, it's a risky business to invest in C#. By the way: who is doing it? There are quite a few well-known examples built on this stack, although it's widely used (as well as Visual Basic). Can you build Docker or Twitch on a .net stack (for those who don't know, these are Go apps)?

If you want to enter B2B apps with your product, you'll need to connect with very specific Microsoft stuff like domains and policies, and as business is conservative, it will not jump off this stack soon. It's kind of painful with any other tech stack, so it's a nice-to-have option.

Even if .net occupies the place for custom apps for just one company, it was a viable option before for companies using the Microsoft stack, and the good news is that now it's a viable option even if you don't want that Microsoft dependency.

entry.title: A Process Map In ASCII Is a Thing
entry.content:
Intro

It started in 2003, I was implementing Axapta or Microsoft Dynamics AX a bit later, and we were modeling the processes in eEPC notation using ARIS Toolset, which was expensive, about 10k USD per user. And it was great for managing changes and documenting the logic, the document flow, although I had some suspicions when we printed the maps on A0 (otherwise they were unreadable) or had 5 levels of decomposition. Could it be simpler – that was the question, but it did the job. About 5 years later I moved on to management consulting, these guys were more cost-aware, so we used eEPC in ARIS Express or flow charts in MS Visio with different notations and yes, in any case it was simpler and still got the job done. In my last effort to model something I chose BPMN 2.0 and Camunda Modeler, because it was free and it was real process modeling with a strict and compact notation.

In Germany companies try to comply with ISO 9001, which says that business processes should be documented, and the simplest form of process flow is used with almost no branches, and it somewhat works for small companies, although I never saw anyone actually using it as a reference. And two times we started ERP implementation it turned out that these process maps hide some important details, to say the least.

Anyway, I had a practical task to write an instruction for us and for a service provider, how we work together. I was discussing some options with an AI chatbot, and the chatbot drew what are called ASCII- or plain-text process maps. Actually it was not the first time, but that time it hit me: I could use it in the document. And yes, I use it a lot myself, I also used it to explain what is going on in conversations with different parties involved and my point is that no one asked a single question – it was that level of simplicity.

The map

Just to illustrate what I mean let's take a look at an example for a "Purchase-to-Pay" process:

Requisition Creation [Requester] (Purchase Requisition)
  |
PR Approval [Approver] (Approved Purchase Requisition)
  |
PO Generation [Procurement Specialist] (Purchase Order)
  |
PO Issued to Vendor [Procurement Specialist] (Purchase Order)
  |
Goods / Service Receipt [Warehouse] (Goods Receipt Note)
  +-> Issues Found [Warehouse] (Return / Dispute Note)
  +-> Accepted
        |
      Invoice Receipt & Matching [Accounting] (Supplier Invoice)
        +-> Mismatch / Hold [Buyer] (Exception Report)
        +-> Verified (3-Way Match Record)
              |
            Payment Processing [Finance] (Payment Advice)

TL;DR: use the following with any chatbot along with the description to get a similar result:

Use [Roles], (Docs), and +-> for branches

The good

I'd name one critical advantage, the accessibility, but it's not that simple, so let's take a look at different perspectives:

  • It's minimal in terms of artificial symbols or colors, so it's easy to read
  • You can use it anywhere for explanation if you can use a monospace font: any document, email or comment
  • There are no graphics, and when graphics are involved, especially something fancy, people are just tired of it and/or suspect BS
  • Normal text search just works
  • You can make small changes without any special tools, just editing the text
  • You can make significant changes with a chatbot relatively easily just by explaining what you want

Now let's take a look at the drawbacks.

The bad

I learned the hard way why the roles, interfaces and documents are important – in fact, a document/information flow can be way more important than functions and branching logic. Having this discipline in mind using ASCII-based process maps is easy, but this may not be the case:

  • There are no conditions for branching and no rules to enforce them
  • Documents are not mandatory and are easy to forget about
  • It's the same for the roles, and the "swim lanes" are non-existent
  • There is no decomposition and I'm not sure whether this approach is scalable at all
  • It's hard to follow if it's more than one process and/or one page long
  • There are no statuses for the documents, so you should just remember not to forget them

Conclusion

There's a surprisingly wide range of online or offline tools to make ASCII process maps, although I would probably write something different. I liked the freedom from any tool I got. It's the same as any text-based format, you can edit it as long as you have a text editor. Some text editors, like Neovim, can make editing these process maps especially convenient, but we will not dig into this rabbit hole. If you are able to set a task for an AI chatbot, it can be very fast as well, and I personally have no problem with showing this process map to a company management at any level. But yes, these maps are not fancy.

entry.title: About Timing
entry.content:
Intro

I understand timing as a planned moment in time when opportunity and ability meet each other. The question that keeps returning to me is this: why is it so hard to get the timing right? It feels mentally and emotionally overwhelming, even though we already know so much about time. Well, let's break it down:

  • What's hard about planning?
  • What's hard when ability is present, but opportunity isn't?
  • What's hard in the opposite case: when opportunity is present, but ability isn't?

A practical example will be looking for a job, as I experienced it myself, and all other examples would be B2B-specific... Ok, just too specific for a broad audience. And we need an appropriate soundtrack, so here it is: "Perfect Timing" by Y'akoto. Let's get into it.

About planning

Should I answer the question of why planning is actually required? Well, it's about probability: from my viewpoint and experience, the chances of opportunity and ability meeting each other accidentally are next to zero. Well, if HRs are bombing your LinkedIn with job offers, they have already evaluated your ability, and they indicate that the opportunity is present. In all other cases, you are welcome to deliberately organize this moment when ability and opportunity are present at the same time (and place, but that's more about logistics, which I will not cover here).

Well, the whole discipline of #project management is actually about two things: planning efforts and executing efforts. Since this reference says next to nothing to most people, I'll try to outline some major issues with planning:

  • You need to evaluate resources, one of which is time, before starting your effort, and that's kind of hard;
  • You need to track dependencies between tasks, which is more technical, but some dependencies are not so obvious; actually, I've encountered situations where assumed dependencies didn't exist much more often;
  • You need buffers for all resources, including time; it doesn't go smoothly all the time, you know.

The planning effort requires some courage – at least to try to look into the future and fail with a 100% probability, but still keep doing it. To stay at peace with planning, a more Confucian way would probably be to accept that it's an iterative process and, as the project management proverb says, the project plan becomes obsolete the moment it's finished. Some recommended study material would be the "Kung-Fu Panda" movies, at least the first three of them. And I'm not even joking.

How long will it take you to land a new job? What tasks does this effort include: updating the CV, finding job postings, applying, passing interviews. Or, in a more advanced content marketing approach, posting some content to attract influencers – sorry, HRs – and letting them offer positions to you. Or maybe finding a consultant and paying them to do whatever it takes to land that job. Or perhaps we should start with market research and figure out what career path we should take.

You see the problem here: we are dealing with uncertainty even when we try to decompose our effort, and that's what we can control. In all other cases, uncertainty only grows as soon as external actors are involved. What I mean by an iterative approach is that we should try any of these paths, get feedback from the job market, and adjust our plans. And by adjusting plans, I mean answering two questions: should we adjust plans within the current path, or should we pivot toward another path? Yes, a job search can be especially difficult because of this high uncertainty, which doesn't happen in most projects where we've already decided what we are doing. Anyway, let's move to the next point.

A lack of opportunity

A lack of opportunity applied to the job market means that there isn't enough demand for your competence and/or experience. Some other factors can come into play, which can render both competence and experience irrelevant – an example being a strong bias toward national candidates, which for me personally is understandable.

What are we going to do about it? Well, we have to start planning:

  • What can we change in our present state to become relevant? If possible, we could acquire some skills, certifications, or language fluency.
  • Are there market forecasts indicating things will change so we become relevant in the future? Then we could just wait. Beware though, that the market usually takes it into account as well.
  • If the prospects are grim, should we look at other markets? I mean other geographic locations, remote options working for companies from other countries, or changing profession entirely.

Let's take a step back: we have planning here and we had planning at the beginning, so what's the difference? Well, the truth is that you can't be sure whether the opportunity is present: you start acting and hope to at least get information about it. Another point is that plans don't matter, but actions do, because plans won't give you feedback to act upon, but any action – whether "right" or "wrong" – will. In fact, there is no "right" or "wrong" action; the difference is simply whether you get feedback or not. Following this logic one step further: sometimes, when it's especially difficult to get good feedback, a non-standard or seemingly hopeless action is better than doing nothing. If you ask me, I was acting almost hopelessly, and then I got an offer simply because I didn't stop.

A lack of ability

An example here is when you get a job offer, but you think you are underqualified for the job. Well, there's a risk they'll find out and fire you, so let's talk about risks. Risk management is a great expression and even a standard process in almost any project management framework, but I'll tell you what: it's all about taking risks. First, without taking the opportunity, you'll never find out whether you were actually underqualified. Second, you can make progress and/or deliver results, and people value that. So the truth here is that you might be underqualified in the beginning, but no one (I repeat, no one) will remember that later. So, there's no point in spiraling into self-reflection here – just do the best you can. As a result of my own self-reflection across my professional career, at 40 years old I firmly decided to take more opportunities (and risks), especially when the impact of potential failure is low. Opportunities tend to be time-limited, so take the time you need to decide, but no more than that.

Bonus-track: alcohol, drugs and gaming

I have a friend – and I didn't tell him I was going to write a post about timing – who just casually told me: "You know, I used to drink a bottle of beer after work, and I noticed I can't do anything after that." I have my own experience with gaming, which actually helped me to some extent when the market was pretty dead after the New Year, but I eventually decided to stop just to free up some time. And it felt so strange at first: I had nothing to do, but then new ideas started bubbling up.

My point is that this stuff eats your time, and by doing so, it reduces your opportunity to get the timing right. Again, you need to have some flexibility: when new input arrives, you need to be able to react faster than other candidates. Sure, you can take some time off, but I don't think it's feasible to live with any of these addictions on a permanent basis. What surprised me was that even after half a year of quitting gaming, I still wanted to go back for a couple of months. I just missed those dopamine hits because the game was so enjoyable.

Living with less dopamine should be a topic for a separate article (or a book, though I don't plan on writing one just yet), but heavy reliance on it puts you in a comfort zone and eliminates your sense of urgency. Imagine other candidates who do have that sense of urgency – who is going to win? Sure, the stress is real and it's a problem, but I've found sports to be the only healthy way to deal with it. Please don't tell me you didn't know that already.

So yeah, addictions suck in every regard, no matter how "soft" they might seem.

Conclusions

I know a lot of smart people who are actually unsuccessful in certain areas of life. They know these concepts, but they don't apply them in their own lives. Why? People panic – it's human and understandable. As Viktor Frankl wrote: "Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response." All you need is not to screw that moment up. It's also human to have a will: just breathe and try to be human in this regard as well, instead of a lizard with only run/attack options. An "I'm not a lizard" poster is available in our shop. Just joking – I have more interesting things to do than selling motivational posters. :)

entry.title: Gitea Is a Thing
entry.content:
Requirements

I can't stop looking for a tool for both product management and project management; I even made an effort to build my own. Okay, let's start with project management – what it's actually about:

  • Issue management, which could turn into
  • Risks,
  • Problems,
  • Changes

Besides that, you'd like to have some project artifacts such as statuses and the deliverables themselves. I deliberately didn't mention tasks, because they belong to... well, task management. Still, task management is what a project manager does on a daily basis, so it would be nice to have a tool for that. In building my own tool, I realized that each type of issue requires a special set of fields, although of course technically I store them in one table. Let's take risks, for instance: we need a risk assessment matrix with likelihood and severity.

Issues have a few things in common, though:

  • An automatically assigned ID, ideally easily referenced from other parts of the software
  • A name, just plain text
  • A description, preferably in Markdown (again, with the ability to reference other issues)
  • A discussion for each issue

And if we're talking about managing more than one project, we'd like to group projects into programs and/or portfolios. A program or a portfolio should have its own definition, which boils down to the bullet points above or can be uploaded as documents.

For product management, we need a hierarchy:

  • Theme/Initiative
  • Epic
  • User Stories
  • Tasks

A hierarchy means that items should probably be linked to each other, similar to projects/programs/portfolios. But to describe each of them, we'll need the same components: an ID, a name, a description, and a discussion.

But that's not all; let's talk about storing project or product documents. I'm still messing around with a folder containing 10 versions of the same file, because although version control systems are commonplace in software development, they are rarely used for office documents like contracts or presentations. Looking at this folder with 10 versions makes me sad, because this particular setup multiplies my chances of making a mistake and increases my stress. It also doesn't motivate us to use simpler formats like Markdown or Org, but we'll leave that story for now.

Alternatives

Redmine could be a great solution if you are at peace with Ruby on Rails and its resource usage. Does it make sense to use it for a company? Absolutely. Does it make sense to use it on my personal laptop for juggling my personal tasks? It's too heavy and it's also total overkill. It's also kind of outdated in terms of backend and interface, but you can skip this part if you like. Anyway, B2B is quite conservative when it comes to choosing a tech stack.

My intuition and some research tell me that Go should be a modern choice for the backend of a modern web app. The frontend probably shouldn't be heavy; single-page apps for particular parts are OK, but when they are used everywhere, things feel bloated. And in terms of scalability, I'd like to be able to start with SQLite and migrate to MySQL or Postgres when things start to get serious. Well, Gitea and its open-source fork Forgejo are here to help, as they tick all the boxes. But how do we actually manage a product or a project with them? Doesn't it look like a stretch?

Tags Everywhere

Well, it requires a certain amount of discipline, which I wouldn't expect from large teams, but it's certainly doable with the feature called tags. Every level of a hierarchy or a particular element within it can be a tag. For example, we can have a tag for a problem or an epic. An epic should ideally reference all included user stories, and the user stories should reference their parent epic. I know, it gets messy from here, but it seems to me that no one has ever tried to use this tool this way. I also see a clear path for future development – for example, adding a risk matrix to list all risks and calculate risk values (and highlight them with colors), or building something more convenient for Epic-User Story relationships.

The insight I experienced is that everything is an actionable item – an issue in terms of Gitea/Forgejo. It can be a task, a problem, a user story, or an epic. With Markdown, we can use a structured template for each issue type. Cross-referencing between issues is as easy as it gets. Furthermore, the discussion thread below each item is a critical feature for enhancing collaboration: yes, I want to discuss everything.

Git is not ideal: it struggles with larger files (sometimes presentations happen to be really big), and for contracts, I might have versions in different formats: first in PDF, then in MS Word, then in PDF again. But I am sure these issues are either solvable or minor enough not to prevent us from automating version control and finally stopping emailing files back and forth. This is a big change, obviously. My only hope is that in the far future, Git will be considered part of a basic education. As well as Markdown, by the way.

Conclusion

Does this sound too futuristic to you when you look at Gitea/Forgejo? Sure, it's targeting developers for now, but I see the potential. The scalability and simplicity are great in my opinion, especially with Docker. Plus, there's the ability to switch databases easily. For me, if something is designed well (meaning the creators share my taste), everything just feels right. The interface is light and responsive, comes with a dark theme, and even offers a CLI version (no, I don't use it). I'm managing two personal sets of tasks this way, let's put it that way, and it has already helped reduce my stress and anxiety by bringing in structure. It's so convenient that it's almost invisible to me. And if I want to collaborate with someone, I can just deploy this Docker container to any hosting. It all just clicks together, exactly as it should.

entry.title: What's Wrong With The Server Software
entry.content:
Intro

The picture I see in August of 2026 really makes me sad: we have great technology stacks finally, we figured out that APIs are probably the most important, we have SSO as end-users and do not need to remember the login and password for every site, we even figured out that web interface probably makes the most sense, but we are still somehow in the Middle Ages in terms of how server software is actually used. I get it, to realize the acquired potential takes time. At the same time, it feels like a rollback and even progress denial after COVID, some kind of mental fatigue that stops people from taking new challenges and transforming the B2B digital environment one more time. They have their reasons, so let's get into the big three software types that are actually used:

  • Microsoft Fanclub
  • New Web Fanclub
  • Old Web Fanclub

It's not all that bad, it's usable (and widely used), it solves the problem, but it feels wrong for many reasons which I'll try to set out. More than that, software to fix this is already here, but it misses some new requirements we've got recently because of politics. OK, let's get into it.

Microsoft Fanclub

Before we start talking about Microsoft products, I have to confess: being a Linux-hobbyist myself, I generally don't like Microsoft products, but that's not the whole truth! Willing to solve real world problems, I found out that ERP solutions from Microsoft (from Navision and Damgaard initially, to be fair) work well and companies mainly use Microsoft environments. I learned Microsoft products and implemented them for a while (since 2003), as well as used the most hated Microsoft product, PowerPoint, to make money in consulting. That being said, I passed the stage of religious hatred and I could probably name a few down-to-earth reasons why these products are mediocre from the user perspective. But I'll point out the good as well.

So, let's start with MS Teams. Collaboration via chat and video conferences wasn't a thing before COVID, as some of you may remember, but now it's the spine of communication. The video conference should just work, and it works. It works surprisingly well in Chrome in any Linux distribution, so I was able to attend a big number of video calls while I was looking for a job. The chat is mediocre: settings are really bad, posting and commenting is bad. I just don't understand how the thumbnail of the document half the size of the screen should increase my productivity – I still can't read anything, and I'd prefer just a link. I can use a link, and a great idea is to have all the files stored in one place (OneDrive) and all the apps (including SharePoint) pointing to this one storage. You can also get a link for a channel or a discussion, but the workflow is organized just badly. It's clear that MS Teams is Microsoft Edge trying and failing to render the web pages, so you are supposed to find a button to reload a page. The chat experience overall is a bad trip, especially when you have experienced Slack or Telegram.

MS Teams has a place for files, and it looks exactly like a network folder, but it's more buggy because they reinvented the wheel here. MS Teams has apps, which are basically web apps rendered inside MS Teams. By the way, if you want to place an app in the marketplace, you have to become a certified MS partner. But beware, most administrators uncheck the "allow third-party apps" setting, so you enjoy a Microsoft-only app store. And due to licensing, you can use Planner for task management in the web version, but you can't use Planner in MS Teams, although MS Teams is actually a browser rendering web apps...

OK, you know what you want – a website with a clear structure, descriptions for links, bullets, tables – you are ready for SharePoint. It works for simple tasks, again being slow and buggy, especially when editing content. I refuse to believe it's a technology from this century; it looks more like the 1990s with a modern design to me, but anyway.

MS online office products, on the other hand, work surprisingly well for collaboration. They are not buggy, they are reasonably lightweight, they lack some functions, and they don't care about 1:1 compatibility with the desktop version. So documents don't look the same, fonts are often a mess, but it solves the problem. I think when they stopped caring about 1:1 exact appearance as on the desktop, it was a pivotal point and it got better. I still prefer to edit the first draft on the desktop version and then upload it, because it's more convenient.

With this wide line of products – from office apps to ERP systems – Microsoft somehow managed to miss the whole middle segment of very useful apps: task management, knowledge base, workflow management, project management and so on. Maybe they don't want to compete with existing products, but at some point you'll have to search for these products and integrate them into the Microsoft ecosystem, which can be painful, because Microsoft invented its own whole world of domains and permissions, which nobody else can understand. How to get it? In Microsoft's world, you need to invest some money to become a certified partner and get access to the products, environments, and documentation.

Frankly speaking, I don't get why anyone would use a Windows environment at this point. Just to have "fun" with domains? Especially when ERP systems are web-based and work in Chrome on any platform. OK, it's not tested yet – we need a couple more centuries to figure this out.

New Web Fanclub

Notion, Asana, Atlassian, JetBrains, and the web applications inspired by them in my opinion belong to the "New Web". They figured out a lot, they use reasonably modern tech stacks (a too modern tech stack can be a problem), they found highly valuable niches to automate, and they work really well. They also have APIs. My problem here is how they are used: I've seen a real employee copying and pasting data from a spreadsheet into one of these apps. And I have an answer to the question: what else should they do to solve this? Stress the importance of APIs and integration more? Give more non-technical presentations about the importance of integration and automation of the end-to-end workflow vs. automation of isolated functions? Maybe create a new integration standard, so integration would be nearly plug-and-play and we could finally avoid copy-pasting and the human errors and frustration associated with it? I don't really know, the fact is that we are all fascinated with these apps, we use them happily, and we switch between windows and copy-paste the same data. If you ask me what should be this one app where the seamless process flow should take place – I'll say: I don't know. Their value lies to such an extent in the front-end that it feels catastrophic to lose it by hiding it under some other app. But the key to the flow state is clearly one interface, at least for one process.

Old Web Fanclub

I'm old enough to remember my sincere love for the good old web apps like Mantis and DokuWiki: simple, fast, well-designed, and... outdated. Pumping them up with plugins to bring them up to date (authentication and design) feels like... OK, I'll not use this metaphor here. :) I googled, I asked AI, and the place is just empty – there's nothing else so convenient. We could probably rewrite them using modern tech stacks and design templates, but nobody is there to do it. Why would you invest a lot of time to rewrite it and offer it as open source if someone else is already selling something like this as a subscription? Or the task to just rewrite them seems not challenging enough – we need more functions. But their simplicity was the key. In terms of integration again, they should be API-first. But I think both aforementioned apps deserve to become just the standard bug tracking and wiki module respectively in some future integrated apps infrastructure.

What's next

Probably one integrated environment would be logical, right? And we have a few attempts to do exactly that. ClickUp and Monday.com are trying to do it. First, I haven't used these products – I hope they deliver what they promise. The idea of flow inside one app is there, though I can't say how well it's implemented. And then politics kick in: although both companies have EU infrastructure for GDPR compliance, American companies are out of fashion in the EU. And also the EU government rightfully presumes that it's better to rely on open source products. So closed source, especially in the cloud, is out of fashion too. There are some attempts, notably OpenProject, but it's not the environment – they are still at the "single project management app" stage. For a project of this scale you need investments, which the USA has or which the EU government could deliver. The problem with investments from the government is that they always leave questions and are mostly ineffective.

Nextcloud is another example – it's basically a file-sharing solution, but its app store is promising. Workflow automation is there, task management is there, document signing is also there, and they also have integrations with existing solutions like the aforementioned OpenProject. It's the best bet for the EU probably, and it would be logical to invest in it, right? And it's actually already happening, as well as implementations for EU government and governmental structures of several EU countries. What disappoints me personally still is this starting with file sharing – starting with an intranet / website / SharePoint alternative would be more logical, but maybe they know better. And it's open source with cloud and on-premise options, so all checks here. I'm also not sure, but it seems to be built around bureaucratic processes – it's heavily focused on file approvals. It breaks my logic a little bit, and also: why so much focus on approvals? Probably that's what governmental structures mostly do...

Conclusion

Intranet, knowledge sharing, simple websites – these are the low-hanging fruits for me whenever I start an automation in any company, and it has served me well. It's standard, simple, safe, and I expect any groupware or solution for online collaboration to be centered around this concept, or at least have a major feature to share information by publishing it. Microsoft got many things wrong, but they surprisingly got it right with SharePoint and invested in it enough to make it usable. They also made it surprisingly extendable and scalable, so some companies build and sell CRM or DMS (I mean document management) or basically any workflow automation based on SharePoint – like, why not. Wiki is probably a better approach to information sharing than a site builder (or CMS, content management system); the problem is that existing solutions are outdated, the most modern being XWiki and Wiki.js. On the one hand, it feels like there's a lack of fresh air here; on the other hand, site builders are not dead, and I had a great time with Drupal, which integrates a publishing workflow, by the way. Or we really need something a little bit more flexible, like static site generators, which could be integrated into other products. I don't know, maybe everybody is using Astro or Strapi in custom software and just not sharing it.

Another way to say what gives me an ick – maybe we need some high-level approach to integration between apps, because we already have great separate products and integration obviously multiplies their potential. The way it's going on now is that every product has its own documented API, but every API is unique. Maybe we should have standards for product types: wiki, workflow automation, DMS, CMS, task management, project management, and so on. Like, if you want, you can extend it, but please support the basic functions. Standards have always moved the industry forward, starting with HTTP or even earlier. And UI/UX is important too: maybe we should have a standard for an application look, not in the form of one CSS, but more in a document describing acceptable principles and guidelines for how the app looks and how the user is supposed to interact with it. And then maybe an integrating app with a marketplace will follow, or some existing solution like Nextcloud will naturally adopt and support these standards.

entry.title: Helldivers 2 and Self-Improvement
entry.content:
Intro

Helldivers 2 is a phenomenon for me as a game. It depicts a futuristic world of "Super Earth-based managed democracy," bringing liberty and democracy to distant worlds using weapons and pumping oil as part of the process. The developers predicted the future by building the most absurd reality possible, joking all the way. The gameplay is surprisingly great, even while being goofy and buggy; fighting bugs with a machine gun is immensely satisfying. I do not play other games, and it is my way of getting in touch with real people and feeling a sense of camaraderie during missions. However, one thought kept disturbing me: this game is surprisingly metaphorical in the sense of self-development. The fun factor itself is connected to specific challenges, and that is exactly what I am going to discuss here.

Diving

The concept of "diving" justifies having multiple lives in the game, which in this imaginary future is made possible with clones. On each mission, a team of four Helldivers or fewer is sent to a planet full of enemies (literally thousands), and when a character dies, a substitute is sent in. I associated this with the idea of reincarnation and accepting the world with all its drawbacks. If reincarnation exists and we are sent to the same world repeatedly, maybe we should start understanding something – or at least learn how to deal with the world and its problems. There is no way out; if you don't handle it, you simply don't play the game.

When you start, you suck, but you eventually get familiar with the weapons and the (awkward) controls. The key to success is also playing as a team: complementing your mates, helping each other, and sharing limited resources. In this regard, this game isn't different from the real world, but in the real world, we often "suck" without maturing – just concentrating on the suffering. We do not value teamwork and the evident necessity to share limited resources, at least for practical reasons. When that realization struck me, I stepped away from the computer like, "What the heck..."

Challenging yourself

The game has difficulty levels from 1 to 10, and the difference between levels is significant, with many more enemies – including heavily armored and armed ones – especially between levels 5 and 6. The point is that once you play at a certain level, it becomes boring. Again, in the game, it is very clear that you need to move to higher difficulty levels. Still, the idea of constantly challenging yourself is not so evident or widely accepted in real life, but that is what happens: life becomes boring.

Self-reflecting

Can I play at this level? Well, you won't get the answer until you try. Sometimes I go back to easier levels in the game, but mostly I am surprised that even when I thought I "sucked," we still finished the mission and all the objectives. It's like, "Do you mean I didn't suck?" It doesn't matter; what matters is if the mission was finished successfully and the spirit of camaraderie was there, along with all the positive vibes. I realized I had false criteria, because this "do I suck" metric is subjective, too focused on myself, and too distorting.

Let’s look at this differently: three guys are playing the game, I joined and killed some enemies, so I contributed and did what I could. You would never hear from the team "you shouldn't be here" or "you didn't contribute enough." Why do we say this in real life? Probably because we are not enjoying the "game." Twice, I joined a game and accidentally killed other characters with my hell-pod. No critique: "It's fine." Once, I drove a vehicle with the others directly into a deep hole and we all got killed. The reaction? "LOL." And it works, because you play worse when you think too much about your previous mistakes. Yet, we continue to criticize each other and feel ashamed in real life. Isn't it strange?

Conclusion

There was one video titled "HD2 is so realistic we had PTSD." Of course, it’s an exaggeration and the guys were just having fun. The thing is that a lot of people have a kind of trauma from the constant flow of negative news and predictions that the world is coming to an end tomorrow. Is it good to escape this world? It kind of works for me, and it works surprisingly well when this fantasy world is worse and more absurd than the one we have now. No, I am not sponsored by Sony or Arrowhead, and I would not recommend HD2 to everyone. My current theory is that it attracts specific types of people who find something in chaos and challenges. Maybe men just need epic moments sometimes.
